strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: FlexiCodec pushes neural audio codecs to very low average frame rates (down to 3Hz controllable, 6.25Hz evaluated), an underexplored regime, and identifies a concrete failure mode (semantic information loss) of fixed-rate low-fps codecs.

The dynamic frame rate mechanism via ASR-feature-guided frame merging is simple, deterministic, interpretable, and supports inference-time controllable rates — a practically useful feature, supported by a compelling correlation analysis (Figure 4) with phoneme rate.

Comprehensive and mostly fair experimental design: baselines (DAC, DualCodec) were retrained at each target frame rate with matched codebook sizes; extensive ablations cover the merging/unmerging transformers, FSQ vs. VQ, and choice of semantic feature (ASR vs. SSL), which strengthens the attribution of gains to the proposed design.

Multiple downstream validations (LM-based TTS with AR+NAR flow matching, ASR probing, XARES audio understanding suite) go beyond codec reconstruction metrics, and the finding that lower AR frame rates do not necessarily hurt TTS quality is interesting.
Detailed reproducibility information: full training configs, loss weights, parameter breakdowns, stride settings for retrained baselines, and a code release commitment.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the overall design closely follows DualCodec (dual-stream, semantic RVQ-1 vs. acoustic RVQ-rest), and dynamic frame merging reuses ideas from DynTok/ToMe/CodecSlime/TFC; the main new ingredients are the ASR-feature-guided merging criterion and the transformer-based merge/unmerge refinement, which are relatively straightforward.

Heavy dependence on a specific frozen ASR encoder (SenseVoice-Small) raises questions about generality: results are English-only, and ablations show SSL features degrade badly in this framework (WER 27.3 with w2v-bert-2), suggesting the method is sensitive to the choice of semantic feature extractor; multilingual and streaming support are left as future work.

Evaluation scope is narrow: codec metrics are computed only on LibriSpeech-test-clean (read English speech, 1,088 clips); the τ thresholds for the reported 8.3Hz/6.25Hz operating points were tuned on the test set; dynamic frame rate's claimed advantage on real-world, silence-heavy data is acknowledged but not actually tested.

WER measured via a single ASR model is the primary semantic metric, which can be circular given the codec is built on a (different) ASR feature; no variance/statistical significance reporting, and the subjective TTS MOS uses only 10 audios x 6 raters per system.

Acoustic quality of FlexiCodec only marginally outperforms the retrained DualCodec baseline (Table 4 shows essentially no acoustic gain from dynamic rate), so the headline benefit is confined to the semantic stream; the claim of 'state-of-the-art audio quality at various bitrate levels' in Section 4.4 overstates fairly modest PESQ/UTMOS differences.

Some writing/consistency issues (e.g., 'one of first' hedging vs. 'first work' claims in abstract, minor typos) and the unmerging module (100M params) plus two merging transformers add significant model complexity relative to baselines, which somewhat weakens the efficiency narrative.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant and underexplored problem (sub-10Hz neural audio codecs for speech LMs) and the motivation—semantic information loss at very low frame rates—is empirically well supported (Figure 3a shows baseline WER degrading from ~5.9% to 31.5% at 6.25Hz).

Comprehensive evaluation: codec metrics at matched bitrates against many open-source codecs (Table 5), ablations of dynamic frame rate (Tables 3-4), component-level ablations (Table 8), ASR probing, XARES audio understanding tasks (Table 7), and a downstream TTS system with both objective and subjective metrics (Table 6).

The dynamic frame rate analysis is informative: the correlation between FlexiCodec frame rate and phoneme rate (Pearson r=0.775, Figure 4) and the TIMIT alignment visualizations (Figure 5) give qualitative insight into what is merged.
Training details, hyperparameters, and baseline retraining configurations are documented thoroughly, supporting reproducibility; code release is promised.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core mechanism: adjacent-frame cosine-similarity threshold merging is essentially the ToMe/DynTok recipe applied to codec features, and dynamic-rate codecs already exist (CodecSlime, TFC, VARSTok, Dieleman et al.). The main new ingredient—using ASR features to guide merging and encoding—is an incremental combination of known parts, and the paper's own ablation (Appendix D / Section 4.2) shows most of the semantic gain comes from swapping in the ASR feature (WER 6.0% at 6.25Hz by simply changing DualCodec's SSL to ASR features), while dynamic frame rate contributes a comparatively modest relative improvement (26% at 6.25Hz).

A methodological flaw: the merging thresholds τ (1.0, 0.91, 0.867) were 'determined based on trial runs on our test set' (Section 4.1), i.e., tuned on evaluation data. This biases comparisons against fixed-rate baselines and undermines the headline results; the effect size of dynamic frame rate could shrink with held-out threshold selection.

Heavy dependence on a single frozen, English-centric ASR encoder (SenseVoice-Small) for both semantics and merging boundaries. This limits generality (no multilingual or code-switched evaluation, acknowledged in Appendix H), prevents streaming, and raises questions about whether 'semantic preservation' is being measured largely through a pipeline aligned with the very ASR model used to build the tokens (potential circularity in WER-based evaluation).

Evaluation scope is narrow: codec metrics on only 1,088 audios from LibriSpeech test-clean; no statistical significance testing for any comparison; subjective TTS evaluation is tiny (6 listeners × 10 audios per system), and FlexiCodec-TTS MOS scores are comparable-to-lower than baselines with the speedup being the main selling point.

The controllable frame rate claim is overstated: at 3Hz the RVQ-1 WER degrades to 51.5% (Table 2), so the '3 to 12.5Hz' range is only usable in a limited quality regime; also the unmerging decoder still operates at fixed 12.5Hz, so downstream NAR modules cannot consume dynamic-rate tokens directly.

Several presentation issues: the demo link in the abstract is empty, the code release is promised only 'after the review period' (cannot be verified), some claims are hedged imprecisely ('the one of first neural audio codecs under 10Hz'), and Figure 3'sτ per-audio frame rate scatter shows high variance around the fitted line, suggesting utterance-level rate control is coarse.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: pushing neural audio codecs below 10Hz is a relevant and underexplored problem for speech language models, and the proposed solution (dynamic frame merging guided by ASR features) is a sensible and novel combination for this regime.

Technically sound and clearly described architecture: the dual-stream (ASR semantic + waveform acoustic) encoding, threshold-based frame merging with learned refinement, and frame unmerging for fixed-rate decoding are all explained in enough detail to reproduce.

Comprehensive evaluation: comparisons against retrained low-frame-rate DAC/DualCodec baselines at matched bitrates (Fig. 3), bitrate-consistent comparisons with many open-source codecs (Table 5), dedicated analysis of the dynamic rate mechanism (Fig. 4, Tables 2-4), extensive component ablations (Table 8), and two downstream applications (TTS in Appendix B, audio understanding in Appendix C).

The dynamic frame rate ablation (Tables 3-4) and the phoneme-rate correlation analysis (Fig. 4) convincingly support the central claim that adaptive frame allocation preserves semantics at very low average rates, with large WER gains (e.g., 4.15% vs 31.5% at 6.25Hz for RVQ-1).

The controllable frame rate property (3-12.5Hz from one model) and the demonstration of competitive TTS with substantial RTF speedups are practical, useful contributions; limitations (English-only, non-streaming) are honestly discussed.
Reproducibility is addressed well: training configs, loss weights, parameter breakdowns, baseline retraining recipes, and a code release commitment.
weaknesses: Heavy dependence on a frozen, large ASR model (SenseVoice-Small, 300k hours) for both semantic encoding and merging boundaries ties semantic tokens to that model's biases and language coverage; the approach is likely fragile for multilingual/noisy domains, and the paper leaves this unexplored.

Some test-set tuning is admitted: the τ settings for evaluation (0.91, 0.867) were 'determined based on trial runs on our test set,' which risks optimistic evaluation; a validation-set protocol would be cleaner.

Codec evaluation is restricted to LibriSpeech test-clean (read, clean English speech, 1,088 clips); the authors themselves note dynamic merging may benefit even more on real-world audio with silence, but this is not tested. Subjective TTS evaluation is also small-scale (10 audios, 6 raters per system).

Component novelty is incremental: the method is largely a composition of existing ideas (DualCodec-style dual streams, DynTok-inspired similarity-based merging, ToMe-style token merging, FSQ), and the paper's contribution is primarily empirical/system-level rather than conceptual; 'one of first codecs under 10Hz' is a slightly vague superiority claim given TaDiCodec/TASTE also operate below 10Hz (though they need text).

Acoustic quality at 6.25Hz degrades noticeably (PESQ 2.76, SIM 0.71), and the 12.5Hz NAR TTS variant is clearly worse than the 50Hz NAR variant, limiting the end-to-end speed story; also, retrained baselines, while carefully configured, are still the authors' own versions rather than community-validated systems.

The merging threshold governs a discrete, non-differentiable decision, and the maximum merge length (8 frames) plus utterance-level (non-streaming) processing constrain applicability to real-time use; these practical restrictions are only briefly discussed.

strengths: Clear and relevant problem: pushing neural audio codecs below 12.5Hz toward text-like frame rates for speech LMs is an active and important direction, and the paper is among the first to demonstrate high-quality reconstruction at ~6Hz average frame rate with controllable rates (3-12.5Hz).

Comprehensive evaluation: semantic tests (WER on RVQ-1, RVQ1:8, and an ASR probing task), acoustic tests (PESQ, MCD, SIM, UTMOS), bitrate-matched comparisons with many open-source codecs, retrained baselines at 12.5/8.3/6.25Hz, downstream TTS, audio-understanding probing, OOD/multilingual generalization, and efficiency (RTF) benchmarks.

Thorough ablations, including a factorial analysis (Table 9) that separates the contributions of the ASR feature source, dynamic frame rate, merging/unmerging transformers, and FSQ, plus qualitative visualization showing merged tokens align with syllables/long vowels/silence (Figure 5).

The system is practical: low RTF (0.018 encode / 0.006 decode), no transcripts required during training, and a full AR+NAR TTS implementation demonstrating real downstream utility with significant speedups (e.g., 7.3x AR speedup over CosyVoice).
Well-organized paper with detailed implementation configurations in appendices, supporting reproducibility; code and demos are claimed to be released.
weaknesses: Core novelty is largely a combination of existing components: dual-stream encoding (DualCodec), ASR-feature semantics (XY-Tokenizer, SpeechTokenizer), token merging (ToMe/DynTok/CodecSlime), and FSQ. The genuinely new element — greedy cosine-similarity-threshold frame merging guided by ASR features — is a simple heuristic with no learnable component, and the authors themselves frame a learnable merging module as future work.

The headline gains are unevenly attributable: the factorial analysis shows the SSL→ASR feature switch accounts for the bulk of semantic improvement (WER 31.5→5.99), while the dynamic frame rate mechanism (the paper's central claimed contribution) yields a comparatively modest gain (5.99→4.15, ~30% relative, with much smaller gains on RVQ1:8 and acoustic metrics).

Fairness concerns in baseline comparisons: FlexiCodec leverages a frozen SenseVoice ASR model trained on 300k hours as an external semantic feature extractor, while retrained baselines (DAC, DualCodec) do not receive a comparably strong augmentation; the merged-frame length attributes also add overhead that complicates bitrate accounting.

The frame-rate-specific merging thresholds (τ = 1.0, 0.91, 0.867) were tuned via trial runs on the test set, which risks overfitting to the evaluation data; evaluation is also limited to a single relatively clean test set (LibriSpeech-test-clean, 1,088 audios) for the main results, with no confidence intervals or significance tests anywhere.

Multilingual results are weak for the semantic stream (WER(RVQ1) of 100% on Chinese/Korean/French), revealing that the core semantic representation is heavily English-specific; this limits the generality of the approach and contradicts the broad applicability framing, though it is honestly reported.

Subjective MOS evaluation is small-scale (10 audios per system, 6 raters), and several claims (e.g., 'state-of-the-art audio quality at various bitrates') are stronger than the modest margins over DualCodec would strictly support; acoustic quality at 6.25Hz degrades notably (PESQ 2.76 vs GT 4.5).

strengths: The paper targets an under-explored regime (below 10Hz average frame rate) for neural audio codecs, and the controllable frame-rate property (3-12.5Hz from a single model) is a genuinely useful and distinctive feature for downstream efficiency trade-offs.

The evaluation is fairly comprehensive: semantic (WER on RVQ-1 and RVQ1:8, ASR probing), acoustic (PESQ, MCD, SIM, UTMOS), efficiency (RTF), TTS downstream with both objective and subjective metrics, audio understanding probing, OOD English and multilingual generalization, and multiple ablations including a factorial analysis of design choices.

The dynamic frame rate analysis (Figure 4 correlation with phoneme rate, Table 2 threshold-rate-WER trade-off, Table 3/4 fixed-rate vs. dynamic-rate ablations) is a thoughtful attempt to characterize the mechanism rather than just report end numbers.
The retrained low-frame-rate baselines (DAC, DualCodec at 12.5/8.3/6.25Hz) fill a real gap since no open-source below-12.5Hz baselines exist, and configurations are documented in the appendix.
Reproducibility support is good: training details, loss weights, parameter breakdowns, baseline stride configurations, and released code/demos.
weaknesses: The headline claim of superior semantic preservation is substantially driven by borrowing features from a frozen, 300k-hour SenseVoice ASR encoder, and the paper's own factorial analysis (Table 9) makes this explicit: switching SSL to ASR features alone improves RVQ1 WER from 31.5 to 5.99, whereas the paper's titular contribution (dynamic frame rate) accounts for a much smaller 4.43->4.15 (~6% relative) improvement. The core novelty is therefore a modest increment on top of a powerful external representation.

There is a circularity concern in the evaluation: semantic preservation is measured primarily via ASR WER, and the semantic tokens are distilled from a strong ASR model's features. The WER gains may largely reflect transplanted ASR performance rather than genuine codec-level semantic learning; a fairer comparison would need to hold the feature extractor fixed across systems or use semantic metrics not aligned with the supervision signal.

The dynamic frame merging mechanism is algorithmically simple: a greedy left-to-right adjacent-frame cosine similarity threshold, essentially DynTok/ToMe applied to codec features. The Transformer refinement and unmerging modules are sensible engineering but not conceptually new. The overall contribution reads as a combination of known components (DualCodec-style dual streams, DynTok-style merging, FSQ, quantizer dropout).

Key baselines are retrained by the authors rather than evaluated from official checkpoints, and even the fixed-rate FlexiCodec variants are derived from the proposed system; this asymmetry raises concerns about baseline tuning effort, though the recipe documentation partially mitigates it.

Threshold values tau used for evaluation (1.0/0.91/0.867) were 'determined based on trial runs on our test set,' which constitutes tuning on test data; the same applies to per-language tau selection in the multilingual experiments.

The TTS human evaluation is small (six evaluators, 10 audios per system) and the confidence intervals in Table 6 are wide; differences between configurations (e.g., NMOS 3.22-3.32) may not be statistically meaningful.

Experiments are essentially single-dataset (LibriLight/LibriSpeech, English audiobook-style speech); the OOD and multilingual analyses in Appendix F show clear degradation (e.g., 100% WER on several languages zero-shot) and are relegated to the appendix rather than treated as a first-class limitation.

The acoustic quality contribution is weak: Table 4 shows dynamic frame rate provides essentially no PESQ/UTMOS gain over fixed-rate variants, and the MCD/SIM gaps are small, so the practical benefit is confined to semantic metrics and controllability, a narrower impact than the abstract implies.

Some important comparisons are missing or handicapped: CodecSlime and TFC/VARSTok (the closest dynamic-rate codecs) are discussed but not empirically compared, and XY-Tokenizer is acknowledged as concurrent but appears in only some tables with missing RVQ-1 results.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: the paper identifies concrete reasons (insufficient semantic decoupling and loss of transient phonetic detail) why fixed-rate codecs degrade below 12.5Hz, and addresses both with a principled design (ASR-feature-assisted dual-stream encoding plus dynamic frame merging).

Strong empirical evaluation: comparisons against many open-source codecs at bitrate-matched operating points (Table 5), retrained low-frame-rate baselines (DAC, DualCodec) with matched codebook sizes, out-of-domain (Emilia) and multilingual tests, and downstream TTS with both objective metrics and human MOS evaluations.

Comprehensive ablation and analysis: the factorial analysis (Table 9) cleanly isolates the contribution of each design choice, showing that switching SSL->ASR features is the dominant factor (31.5->5.99 WER) and that dynamic frame rate gives consistent further gains; the phoneme-rate correlation analysis (Figure 4) and token-phoneme alignment visualizations (Appendix A) provide good mechanistic insight.

A practically valuable feature: a single model supports inference-time controllable frame rates from 3Hz to 12.5Hz, and the codec achieves high-quality reconstruction at average frame rates below 10Hz, which the authors convincingly position as a frontier for reconstructible codecs.

Good reproducibility posture: training details, hyperparameters, stride configurations for retrained baselines, loss weights, and parameter breakdowns are provided; code and audio demos are promised, and limitations/future work are candidly discussed (Appendix J).
weaknesses: Merging threshold values used for the headline 8.3Hz/6.25Hz evaluations (tau=0.91, 0.867) were 'determined based on trial runs on our test set', which constitutes mild test-set tuning; a validation-set protocol should be used and its sensitivity reported.

Heavy dependence on a specific frozen ASR model (SenseVoice-Small): the semantic tokens and merging boundaries inherit the ASR model's language bias. This is evident in the multilingual results where WER(RVQ1) is 100% for ZH/KO, so the core 'semantic' stream is essentially English-ASR-specific; the implications for multilingual speech LLMs are not fully explored.

The core mechanism (merging semantically similar adjacent frames guided by a pretrained encoder's feature similarity) is closely related to DynTok, CodecSlime, TFC, VARSTok, and syllable-unit discovery; the novelty is mainly in applying it to the very-low-frame-rate regime with ASR guidance and integrated reconstruction, which is somewhat incremental.

The absolute gains from dynamic frame rate are moderate for some metrics (e.g., +8% relative RVQ1:8 WER, ~0.05-0.09 SIM), and acoustic metrics show essentially no benefit (PESQ/UTMOS unchanged in Table 4), so the headline claim rests mainly on RVQ1 semantic WER.

The unmerging module must deterministically reconstruct fixed 12.5Hz structure from merged frames, which caps acoustic fidelity (PESQ ~2.76 vs. GT 4.5 at 6.25Hz); no listening test is provided for codec reconstruction quality itself, only objective metrics.

Some baselines are retrained by the authors, which is commendable but makes it hard to rule out sub-optimal baseline tuning; also FlexiCodec has notably more parameters (216M trainable, 289M encode) than many compared codecs, and the ASR encoder (234M frozen) is part of the practical deployment cost.
